title: Effect of Concentration on Rate
content:
# Effect of Concentration on Rate

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Describe how concentration affects reaction rate
- Explain the effect using collision theory
- Interpret graphs showing concentration effects
- Design experiments to investigate concentration effects

## Introduction

**Concentration** is one of the key factors affecting reaction rate. Increasing the concentration of reactants generally increases the rate of reaction. This principle is used extensively in industry and the laboratory.

## Key Concepts

### The Effect

**Increasing concentration increases the rate of reaction.**

- More concentrated solutions contain more particles in the same volume
- More particles = more collisions = faster rate

### Collision Theory Explanation

[DIAGRAM: Two beakers - dilute solution (few particles) vs concentrated solution (many particles)]

**Step-by-step explanation:**
1. Higher concentration = more reactant particles per unit volume
2. Particles are closer together on average
3. This increases the frequency of collisions
4. More collisions per second means more successful collisions per second
5. Therefore, the rate of reaction increases

### Effect on Graphs

**Volume of gas vs time at different concentrations:**

```
Volume of gas (cm³)
    ↑
    |              High conc. ___________
    |             /
    |           /   Medium conc. ___________
    |         /    /
    |       /    /
    |     /    /    Low conc. ___________
    |   /    /     /
    | /    /     /
    |/___/____/_________________________→
                    Time (s)
```

**Key observations:**
- **Steeper initial gradient** = faster initial rate (higher concentration)
- **All lines reach the same final volume** if same amount of limiting reactant
- **Higher concentration finishes first**

### Investigating Concentration - Marble Chips and Acid

**Reaction:**
$$\text{CaCO}_3 + \text{2HCl} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$$

**Variables:**
- Independent variable: Concentration of acid
- Dependent variable: Volume of CO₂ produced (or mass lost)
- Control variables: Mass of marble chips, surface area, temperature, volume of acid

**Method:**
1. Set up gas syringe or balance
2. Add 50 cm³ of 0.5 M HCl to flask
3. Add 5 g marble chips (same size)
4. Start timer and record gas volume every 30 s
5. Repeat with 1.0 M, 1.5 M, and 2.0 M HCl
6. Keep all other variables constant

**Expected results:**
- Higher concentration → steeper curve → faster rate
- All reach same final volume (same mass of CaCO₃)

### Investigating Concentration - Sodium Thiosulfate

**Reaction:**
$$\text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3 + \text{2HCl} \rightarrow \text{2NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{SO}_2 + \text{S}$$

(Sulfur precipitate makes solution cloudy)

**Method - Disappearing cross:**
1. Place flask on paper with black cross
2. Add 50 cm³ of sodium thiosulfate solution
3. Add 5 cm³ of dilute HCl and start timer
4. Time until cross disappears
5. Repeat with different concentrations of sodium thiosulfate
6. Keep total volume constant by adding water

**Example setup:**

| Na₂S₂O₃ (cm³) | Water (cm³) | Total (cm³) | Concentration |
|---------------|-------------|-------------|---------------|
| 50 | 0 | 50 | Highest |
| 40 | 10 | 50 | High |
| 30 | 20 | 50 | Medium |
| 20 | 30 | 50 | Low |
| 10 | 40 | 50 | Lowest |

**Results:**
- Higher concentration = shorter time = faster rate
- Plot concentration vs 1/time (1/time ∝ rate)

### Mathematical Relationship

For many reactions:
$$\text{Rate} \propto \text{concentration}$$

If concentration doubles, rate approximately doubles.

**Graph of rate vs concentration:**
```
Rate
    ↑
    |           /
    |         /
    |       /
    |     /
    |   /
    | /
    |/_______________________→
         Concentration
```

(Often gives a straight line through the origin for simple reactions)

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** Explain, using collision theory, why doubling the concentration of hydrochloric acid approximately doubles the rate of reaction with magnesium.

**Solution:**
- Doubling concentration means twice as many HCl particles per unit volume
- The particles are on average closer together
- There are twice as many collisions per second
- Twice as many successful collisions occur per second
- Therefore the rate approximately doubles

---

**Example 2:** Look at these results for the disappearing cross experiment:

| Concentration (M) | Time (s) | 1/time (s⁻¹) |
|-------------------|----------|---------------|
| 0.1 | 100 | 0.010 |
| 0.2 | 50 | 0.020 |
| 0.3 | 33 | 0.030 |

What pattern do the results show?

**Solution:**
- As concentration increases, time decreases
- The 1/time values (which represent rate) increase
- When concentration doubles (0.1 → 0.2 M), 1/time doubles (0.010 → 0.020)
- Rate is directly proportional to concentration
- This confirms: Rate ∝ concentration

---

**Example 3:** In an experiment, 2M acid produced 50 cm³ of gas in 20 seconds. Predict approximately how long it would take 1M acid to produce 50 cm³ of gas.

**Solution:**
- Rate ∝ concentration
- If concentration halves, rate halves
- Half the rate means twice the time for the same amount of product
- Time ≈ 2 × 20 = **40 seconds**

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Thinking higher concentration produces more product
- **Correct:** Higher concentration produces product FASTER, not more (total product depends on amount of reactant)

- **Mistake:** Not keeping total volume constant when diluting
- **Correct:** Add water to maintain constant volume when comparing concentrations

- **Mistake:** Changing multiple variables at once
- **Correct:** Only change concentration; keep surface area, temperature, etc. constant

## Practice Questions

1. Explain, using collision theory, how increasing concentration increases the rate of reaction. (4 marks)

2. A student investigates the reaction between marble chips and hydrochloric acid using three different concentrations. Sketch the graphs you would expect on the same axes. Label clearly which line represents which concentration. (4 marks)

3. In the disappearing cross experiment:
   a) What is measured? (1 mark)
   b) Why does the solution turn cloudy? (1 mark)
   c) How is rate calculated from the time measured? (1 mark)

4. Design an experiment to investigate how the concentration of sodium thiosulfate affects the rate of its reaction with hydrochloric acid. Include:
   - Method
   - Variables to control
   - How to vary concentration while keeping volume constant
   (6 marks)

5. Explain why all the graphs in a concentration investigation reach the same final volume of gas (if other factors are kept constant). (2 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Concentration | The amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution |
| Independent variable | The variable you deliberately change |
| Dependent variable | The variable you measure |
| Control variables | Variables kept constant to ensure a fair test |
| Proportional | When one quantity doubles, so does the other |

## Summary

- **Increasing concentration increases rate**
- More particles per volume → more collisions → more successful collisions
- On graphs: higher concentration = steeper initial gradient
- All lines reach same final value (same limiting reactant)
- Rate is often proportional to concentration (Rate ∝ [reactant])
- **Key experiment:** Disappearing cross (time until cross disappears)
- Rate = 1/time in disappearing cross experiments
